passages.happening:
The LORD speaks concerning Moab. Its towns are taken and put to shame, Nebo and Kiriathaim among them (verse 1). There is no more praise for Moab; in Heshbon they plot its ruin (verse 2). A cry goes up from Horonaim, devastation and great destruction (verse 3). Moab is broken, and its little ones cry out (verse 4). People are told to run for their lives (verse 6). ‘Because you trust in your works and treasures, you too will be captured’ (verse 7), and Chemosh, Moab's god, will go into exile with his priests and officials.

‘Cursed is the one who is remiss in doing the work of the LORD, and cursed is he who withholds his sword from bloodshed’ (verse 10).

‘Moab has been at ease from youth, settled like wine on its dregs; he has not been poured from vessel to vessel or gone into exile’ (verse 11). So its taste and smell have not changed. The days are coming when God will send men to pour it out and smash its jars (verse 12). ‘Then Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh, just as the house of Israel was ashamed when they trusted in Bethel’ (verse 13). Its warriors are cut down (verses 14 and 15). Its neighbors are told to mourn: how the mighty sceptre is broken (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Moab lay on the high plateau east of the Dead Sea, with good land for grain, vineyards and sheep. Much of what is known of Moab outside the Bible comes from the Mesha Stele, a black basalt inscription found in 1868 at Dhiban, the Dibon of this chapter. Set up around 840 BC by Mesha king of Moab, it credits the god Chemosh with freeing Moab from Israel, and it names several towns that appear here, among them Nebo, Kiriathaim, Dibon, Aroer and Jahaz.

Wine left to sit on its dregs grows thick and stale. Good wine was poured from jar to jar to clear it. Moab had never been poured out, never known exile or upheaval, so its pride had settled and thickened.

The chapter gives no date for Moab's fall. Moab was subject to Babylon in Jeremiah's time and sent envoys to the meeting of western kings in chapter 27.
passages.later: Isaiah also lamented over Moab: ‘my heart laments for Moab like a harp’ (Isaiah 16:11). Zephaniah warned of those in Jerusalem ‘settled in complacency’ (Zephaniah 1:12).
passages.hard:
How can verse 10 curse anyone who holds back the sword from bloodshed, while God himself weeps for Moab?

Verse 10 is one of the harshest lines in Jeremiah, and it sits uneasily beside God's lament in verses 31 to 36. Interpreters read it as a statement about the certainty of God's judgment: the agent God has appointed, in context most likely the Babylonian army, must carry out its task fully, and half-hearted obedience to God's command is itself condemned, as with Saul in 1 Samuel 15. It is not a general command to believers to shed blood. Many readers also point out that the chapter holds together two things the Bible often keeps in tension: God's judgment is real, and God takes no pleasure in it (Ezekiel 18:32). Some find the tension unresolved and say so.

Moab here is an ancient kingdom of the sixth century BC. These notes draw no line from this chapter to any people or state of the present day, and verse 10 gives no one a warrant for violence.
passages.asks: Moab had never been poured from vessel to vessel, and its pride had thickened. Ask whether comfort has let something in you settle and harden. And ask what God might be using to pour you out and clear you.

passages.t: Moab's pride, God's lament, and restoration at the last
passages.happening:
Dibon is told to come down from its glory, and Aroer to ask the fleeing what has happened (verses 18 and 19). Judgment has come on the high plain and town after town is named (verses 21 to 24). ‘The horn of Moab has been cut off, and his arm is broken’ (verse 25). Moab will wallow in its vomit, because it magnified itself against the LORD and laughed at Israel (verses 26 and 27).

‘We have heard of Moab’s pomposity, his exceeding pride and conceit, his proud arrogance and haughtiness of heart’ (verse 29). God knows its insolence, and its boasts are empty (verse 30).

Then God himself grieves. ‘Therefore I will wail for Moab; I will cry out for all of Moab’ (verse 31). He weeps for the vine of Sibmah (verse 32). Joy and gladness are gone from the fields, and no one treads the grapes with shouts (verse 33). ‘Therefore My heart laments like a flute for Moab’ (verse 36). Every head is shaved and every beard cut in mourning (verse 37).

An eagle swoops over Moab (verse 40). Terror, pit and snare wait for it; whoever escapes one falls into the next (verses 43 and 44). Fire goes out from Heshbon (verse 45). ‘Yet in the latter days I will restore Moab from captivity,’ declares the LORD (verse 47). Here ends the judgment on Moab.
passages.hearers:
Much of this chapter echoes Isaiah 15 and 16, the older oracles against Moab. Jeremiah takes up earlier prophecy and applies it again.

The lament of verses 31 to 36 is remarkable. The God who pronounces judgment on Moab weeps over it, and his heart laments like a flute, the instrument played at funerals.

The chapter's last word is restoration. Moab's story is not ended by its judgment. Ruth, the great-grandmother of David, had been a Moabite, and a Moabite woman stands in the line of Israel's kings.
passages.later: Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi, ‘your people will be my people, and your God will be my God’ (Ruth 1:16). Ezekiel says, ‘For I take no pleasure in anyone’s death’ (Ezekiel 18:32).
passages.asks: God judges Moab's pride and weeps for Moab at the same time. Ask what it would look like to grieve over the fall of those who mocked you. And ask what pride in you God might be calling, by its right name, pomposity and conceit.
